title: How Does Your Keyboard Know Which Key You Pressed?
sources: Wikipedia 'Keyboard matrix circuit' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_matrix_circuit): keys sit at the crossings of row and column wires; pressing a key connects one row to one column; a controller scans the matrix to find which crossing is closed; pressing several keys can cause ghosting, which diodes prevent

QMK docs 'How a Keyboard Matrix Works' and 'How Keys Are Registered' (docs.qmk.fm): the firmware scans rows/columns repeatedly, looks up the pressed position and sends a keycode over USB; the operating system turns the keycode into a character using the selected keyboard layout
Wooting 'What influences keyboard input speed' / Stapelberg 'Keyboard input latency' (2021): keyboard firmware scans the matrix hundreds to thousands of times per second
USB HID Usage Tables 1.12 (usb.org hut1_12v2.pdf), Keyboard/Keypad page: usage ID 0x04 = 'Keyboard a and A' — the keyboard sends a position code, not a letter
Wikipedia 'AZERTY': the French AZERTY layout swaps A and Q (and Z and W) compared with QWERTY, so with the layout set to French the key printed A on a QWERTY keyboard types Q

lines.text: How does your keyboard know which key you pressed?
lines.caps: HOW DOES YOUR *KEYBOARD | KNOW WHICH *KEY | YOU *PRESSED?

lines.text: Well, hidden under the keys is a grid of wires,
lines.caps: WELL, *HIDDEN | UNDER THE *KEYS | IS A *GRID OF WIRES

lines.text: rows running across and columns running down.
Press a key, and it connects one row to one column,
lines.caps: *PRESS A KEY | AND IT *CONNECTS | ONE *ROW | TO ONE *COLUMN

lines.text: A little chip checks the rows one by one,
lines.caps: A LITTLE *CHIP | *CHECKS THE ROWS | ONE BY *ONE

lines.text: and the crossing that connects tells it exactly which key it was.
lines.caps: AND THE *CROSSING | THAT *CONNECTS | TELLS IT *EXACTLY | WHICH *KEY IT WAS

lines.text: But here's the twist: your keyboard doesn't know letters.
lines.caps: BUT HERE'S THE *TWIST | YOUR *KEYBOARD | DOESN'T KNOW *LETTERS

lines.text: It just sends a number, like four for the A-key,
lines.caps: IT JUST *SENDS | A *NUMBER | LIKE *4 | FOR THE *A-KEY

lines.text: and your computer decides which letter that means.
So switch the layout to French,
and that same key suddenly types a Q.
Your keyboard never typed a single letter.
It just told your computer where you pressed.
